title: Surface adsorbates suppress low-frequency noise for shallow nitrogen-vacancy centers
authors: Zhiyang Yuan, David A. Fehr, Kalliope Zervas, Sorawis Sangtawesin, Lila V. H. Rodgers, Patryk Gumann, Michael E. Flatte, Nathalie P. de Leon
abstract: Shallow nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are promising nanoscale quantum sensors, yet their coherence is strongly limited by surface-induced noise. Surface adsorbates are widely believed to be a major source of decoherence. Here, we test this assumption by characterizing shallow single NV centers under ultrahigh vacuum (UHV) conditions, where the diamond surface is kept free of adsorbates, and comparing their behavior to ambient conditions. Surprisingly, we observe a ~4x reduction in the Hahn echo coherence time T2 in UHV. By combining Hahn echo measurements in the single-quantum (SQ) and double-quantum (DQ) bases, we separate contributions from different noise sources and find that both electric and magnetic noise are enhanced in UHV. In contrast, T1 measurements reveal an increased DQ T1 in UHV, indicating suppressed electric field noise in the ~100 MHz frequency regime. These results point to a modification of the surface noise spectrum upon adsorbate removal, with different frequency regimes arising from distinct microscopic mechanisms. Specifically, we find that the low frequency noise is consistent with increased surface charge in UHV that can be compensated by surface adsorbates in ambient conditions. Our findings highlight a complex and previously underappreciated role of surface adsorbates in shaping the noise environment of shallow NV centers, with important implications for nanoscale quantum sensing.
summary: The research investigates how surface adsorbates dictate the coherence of NV centers in diamond by comparing measurements in air versus UHV. While initial $T_2$ data suggests adsorbates are crucial, detailed analysis shows that low-frequency noise arises from surface charge compensated by these molecules. This work provides a nuanced understanding of environmental coupling essential for building reliable quantum sensors.
main_problem: The primary goal is understanding how surface adsorbates limit the coherence time ($T_2$) of shallow Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, a key quantum sensor.
main_result: Removing adsorbates by moving to Ultra-High Vacuum (UHV) significantly reduces $T_2$ ($\sim 4	imes$), but analyzing different relaxation channels reveals that the low-frequency noise is linked to surface charge compensated by adsorbates in ambient air.
method: The study uses advanced Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) techniques, including Hahn echo measurements ($T_2$) in both Single-Quantum (SQ) and Double-Quantum (DQ) bases, alongside longitudinal relaxation ($T_1$) measurements, comparing results between ambient air and UHV.
model_or_system: The physical system is a shallow NV center embedded in diamond. The analysis involves separating decoherence contributions into electric and magnetic noise components by utilizing the distinct sensitivities of SQ and DQ spin measurements.
key_observables: $T_2$ coherence time, $T_1$ relaxation times, relative contributions of electric vs. magnetic noise, and noise spectral density power-law exponents ($\alpha$).
important_parameters: The comparison between ambient air and UHV conditions; the frequency regimes (e.g., $\sim 100 	ext{ MHz}$ for $T_1$); and the depth dependence of the noise components.
main_assumptions: The observed changes in coherence are directly attributable to the presence or removal of surface adsorbates, which modify the local electric field environment.
figures_summary: Figures compare $T_2$ measurements (Air vs UHV) showing a large difference; they also detail the decomposition of decoherence rates into electric and magnetic parts across different depths and show $T_1$ comparisons between bases in both environments.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares NV center coherence under ambient versus UHV conditions, uses SQ/DQ measurements to separate noise sources (E vs B), analyzes depth scaling of these noise components, and contrasts the findings from $T_2$ with those from $T_1$.
why_interesting: This work provides critical experimental data on environmental coupling in solid-state qubits. The ability to spectroscopically distinguish between electric and magnetic noise sources using DQ measurements is highly valuable for designing robust quantum memories.

NV sensing of materials.note: The paper directly uses NV centers to probe environmental noise sources ($T_2$ decoherence), which is central to quantum relaxometry and magnetic/noise spectroscopy using spin-defect impurities.
